query: Consider noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements and targeted in a single-phase solid-solution state. Their crystal structure is difficult to control at fixed composition, while unsuccessful formation can involve phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures under synthesis regimes with rapid heating and cooling. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs formation and crystal-structure selection in this regime and why? Define a controlled intervention without specifying a technique, predict the observations relative to the initial single-phase baseline, identify the applicable compositional and processing boundaries, cite supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Synchronization of metal salt decomposition temperatures is key to achieving a homogeneous single-phase HEA by ensuring simultaneous metal ion reduction and nucleation.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-metal salt precursor mixture in which individual metal salts possess disparate thermal decomposition and reduction temperatures.
generation.intervention: Adjust the relative loading and chemical composition of the precursor salts to narrow the gap in their decomposition temperatures.
generation.conditions: Flash heating under rapid decomposition conditions, comparing samples made from the standard precursor ratio and those made using chemically adjusted precursor mixtures designed to achieve a temporal overlap of decomposition events.
generation.structural_mediator: The temporal overlap and synchronization of nucleation events, which drive immediate atomic intermixing.
generation.mechanism: When the decomposition of the individual metal salts is synchronized (i.e., occurring nearly simultaneously), simultaneous reduction and nucleation of all constituent metals occur, resulting in an intimate atomic mixing that promotes single-phase HEA formation. In contrast, asynchronous decomposition leads to sequential reduction that fosters local concentration gradients and phase segregation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples produced from the synchronized precursor mixture will display a more uniform elemental distribution and a higher degree of single-phase alloy formation, whereas those prepared with unsynchronized precursor mixtures will show signs of phase segregation and elemental clustering.
generation.baseline: HEA nanoparticles synthesized from standard precursor mixtures with typical, disparate decomposition temperatures that sometimes result in phase separation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies to precursor systems where chemical tuning is feasible; its effectiveness may be limited if the intrinsic decomposition properties of the salts are too dissimilar to reconcile.
generation.uncertainty: The exact adjustments in precursor loading and composition required for precise synchronization are not fully defined and likely depend on the specific metal combination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA nanoparticles by flash heating: one using the standard precursor mixture and another using an adjusted precursor mixture with modified loading ratios designed to synchronize decomposition temperatures, then compare the outcomes under identical heating conditions.
measurements: Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) to verify convergence in decomposition temperature profiles
X-ray diffraction (XRD) to assess phase purity and detect any secondary phases
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) mapping to evaluate the uniformity of elemental distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the sample synthesized with the synchronized precursor mixture does not exhibit statistically meaningful improvements in elemental homogeneity and single-phase formation compared to the standard sample, then the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: As shown in Table S2, the thermal decomposition of the five metal salts occurs at different temperatures. Figure 3a shows the temperature profile along the depth. Once the thermal decomposition temperature (TD) of the metal precursor is reached but below the melting temperature (TM) of the corresponding metals, the thermal decomposition of the mixed metal salt particles adsorbed on the LIG occurs accompanied by gas release, and then each CrMnFeCoNi nanoparticle with homogeneous composition is generated by nucleation and growth of the species from the decomposition of each mixed metal salt particle. This particle is likely to be at the site of the original metal salt particle (the light green zone in Fig. 3a). When the temperature is above TM while below the boiling temperature (TB) of metals, the metallic elements are in the liquid phase to form molten beads. Since metals are nonwetting with carbon, these liquid metal beads tend to aggregate and grow bigger to minimize their surface energy at high temperatures.
